Smoking promotes atherosclerosis but is not the sole cause. The source does not establish that every smoker develops clinically significant plaque or quantify individual plaque progression.

NHLBI establishes smoking as a contributor to atherosclerotic plaque development, not an inevitable or exclusive cause. The page does not quantify the contribution of each biological mechanism in individual patients.

Coronary plaque buildup is the leading cause of coronary heart disease but not its only mechanism. Coronary microvascular dysfunction and vasospasm can also contribute. The presence of plaque does not necessarily indicate symptomatic disease.

The explicit arterial-wall damage statement appears in the video description rather than a detailed written mechanism. The page does not specify cerebral arterial injury or establish a complete pathway from hypertension to stroke. Additional mechanism-specific evidence is required for LINK2.

The CDC passage does not directly connect hypertension-induced arterial wall damage with cerebral vessel blockage or rupture. The cholesterol-related narrowing mechanism cannot automatically be attributed to hypertension. Additional mechanism-specific evidence is required.

Arterial injury increases stroke risk but does not inevitably result in stroke. Ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke involve different vascular mechanisms. The source does not quantify individual risk or demonstrate that every arterial lesion causes stroke.

The source directly supports CAD as a possible cause of heart muscle weakening but does not establish that every CAD patient develops myocardial injury. It does not specify the extent of injury or a particular heart failure subtype.

Direct evidence establishes myocardial infarction → Heart muscle damage or weakening. Its application to CAD → Heart muscle damage is a conditional pathway through coronary plaque-related infarction rather than proof that CAD always causes myocardial injury. Angina without infarction does not necessarily cause permanent muscle damage.

The evidence specifically supports weakened heart muscle as a mechanism of HFrEF. Heart failure can also occur with preserved ejection fraction through ventricular stiffness. Not every patient with myocardial injury develops heart failure and other causes of HFrEF exist.

This is a mechanistic narrative review, not proof that obesity invariably produces insulin resistance. Mechanisms are multifactorial and the review says that aspects remain incompletely understood. CAUSES here means a contributing mechanism, not a deterministic or sole cause.
The page states increased likelihood, not a direct mechanistic proof that excess adiposity causes insulin resistance in every person. Multiple other risk factors exist.

Insulin resistance alone is not sufficient to establish diabetes; pancreatic insulin secretion and other factors matter. The passage does not imply everyone with insulin resistance develops type 2 diabetes.

Insulin resistance is not sufficient by itself: people can remain normoglycemic with compensatory insulin secretion, and type 2 diabetes is heterogeneous. The assessment is based on the user-supplied Endotext extract; live NCBI page access was blocked during verification.

High blood glucose can cause renal vascular damage but injury is not inevitable in every patient. The page does not describe the detailed cellular mechanism or establish the extent of vascular injury in an individual. High blood pressure is another contributor.

The vascular injury and impaired filtration statements occur in separate passages and their connection is a supported synthesis rather than a detailed step-by-step mechanism. Vascular injury does not inevitably produce diabetic kidney disease. The page does not establish a patient-specific diagnosis or quantify progression.

The passage establishes glucose-related kidney-filter damage and impaired filtration, but it does not explicitly identify the damaged filters as the proposed renal blood-vessel injury or independently establish the exact Damage to kidney blood vessels → Diabetic kidney disease arrow. It provides supporting context rather than complete link-specific evidence.

The inflammatory response occurs in susceptible individuals and is not a universal consequence of allergen exposure. The source supports allergen-triggered airway inflammation rather than proving that allergen exposure initiates asthma as a chronic disease.

The article directly supports inflammatory airway changes and breathing difficulty but does not independently describe these changes as an acute asthma attack or establish the precise inflammation-to-exacerbation relationship. Additional episode-specific evidence is available from K051S02.

Airway inflammation is a contributing mechanism rather than the sole or inevitable cause of an attack. Bronchoconstriction and mucus production can also contribute to airway obstruction. The passage does not establish that inflammation alone is sufficient to produce every asthma exacerbation.

This is a narrative review describing contributory mechanisms rather than demonstrating that all smokers develop persistent airway inflammation or COPD. Other exposures and infections can trigger inflammation. Inflammatory phenotypes and susceptibility differ between individuals.

Airway inflammation is an important contributing mechanism but is not the only cause of airflow limitation in COPD. Alveolar destruction, loss of elastic recoil, protease-antiprotease imbalance and other structural abnormalities also contribute. The review does not establish that inflammation alone is sufficient to produce persistent airflow limitation in every individual.

The source directly establishes smoking-related respiratory damage and inflammatory airway pathology in COPD but does not explicitly demonstrate the intermediate relationship Chronic cigarette smoke exposure → Airway inflammation. Combining these statements would require mechanistic inference. The source is therefore contextual rather than independently sufficient for LINK1.

The source supports hypertension-induced renal vascular narrowing and damage as possible consequences of sustained high blood pressure. It does not establish that every person with hypertension develops renal vascular injury or quantify the duration required. Other conditions can also damage renal vessels.

The evidence supports renal vascular injury as a contributing mechanism of impaired kidney function and potentially chronic kidney disease. It does not establish that every vascular injury causes clinically diagnosed CKD. Reduced filtration alone does not necessarily establish CKD without appropriate evidence of chronicity. Kidney disease can also worsen hypertension, creating a bidirectional relationship.

The source directly establishes renal vascular and filtering-system injury as contributors to impaired filtration. However, it does not explicitly establish renal blood vessel narrowing, which is part of the exact LINK2 intermediate node Damage and narrowing of kidney blood vessels. It therefore provides strong supporting context but not complete independent verification of the fully specified intermediate. Its original question-level partial decision is not automatically changed.

The NHLBI passage describes clot formation in the heart without explicitly naming the atrial chamber. Atrial localization is independently established by K054S01. Not every patient with atrial fibrillation develops an atrial thrombus and clot formation is not inevitable.

Atrial fibrillation increases the likelihood of atrial thrombus formation but does not guarantee it. The passage describes a possible complication rather than demonstrating that all atrial fibrillation episodes produce thrombosis.

Atrial thrombus formation alone does not necessarily cause stroke. The clot or a fragment must embolize into the cerebral circulation and obstruct an artery. Not every atrial thrombus embolizes, and the source does not establish that all atrial fibrillation patients experience ischemic stroke. This mechanism must not be generalized to hemorrhagic stroke.

The source directly supports blood clot embolization and cerebral artery obstruction as a mechanism of ischemic stroke. However, it does not explicitly identify a thrombus formed within the atria as the origin of the embolus. Therefore it is contextual corroboration rather than independently sufficient evidence for the exact Atrial thrombus formation → Cardioembolic ischemic stroke link. The original question-level review decision is not automatically changed.

Direct evidence supports TBI causing structural brain injury, but the full composite effect node also requires epileptogenic remodeling. Scarring, hemorrhage or contusion alone does not establish abnormal epileptic circuit formation. The relationship therefore remains partial for the exact LINK1 outcome.

The source establishes a possible post-traumatic mechanism rather than inevitable epileptogenesis after every TBI. Many injured individuals do not develop epilepsy. Several molecular mechanisms are supported mainly by preclinical models, and their individual causal contributions in humans remain incompletely validated.

The mechanisms increase susceptibility but do not guarantee PTE. Evidence for specific cellular remodeling pathways is partly derived from animal studies and may not be fully established in humans. Early provoked post-traumatic seizures within seven days should not be treated as equivalent to later unprovoked seizures or established PTE. Not every structural brain lesion becomes epileptogenic.

The source supports post-injury abnormal neural connections as a possible seizure mechanism, but does not explicitly establish that the proposed composite intermediate causes higher risk of late unprovoked recurrent seizures specifically classified as post-traumatic epilepsy. Its generic seizure discussion must not be substituted for the more specific PTE evidence.

Active pulmonary TB can produce tissue destruction and fibrosis, but the extent and type of injury vary considerably. Not every patient develops cavitation or permanent scarring. Specific immune mechanisms are incompletely established and some mechanistic evidence derives from animal models. This source establishes a possible structural injury pathway rather than inevitable permanent lung damage.

Although physiologically plausible mechanisms are discussed, the review does not establish that residual structural damage independently causes later impairment in all cases. Much of the epidemiological evidence is observational, baseline lung function is often unavailable, and the authors acknowledge incomplete understanding of the causal mechanisms. The relation is therefore recorded as ASSOCIATED_WITH rather than a confirmed CAUSES arrow.

The review explicitly states that causal pathways underlying PTLD remain poorly understood. Structural abnormalities, lung-function impairment and symptoms vary considerably and do not always correlate closely. Smoking, environmental exposures, comorbidities, deconditioning and other factors may contribute to impairment. The source supports association rather than an independently established causal effect of scarring on persistent respiratory limitation.

The detailed passage describes a general pneumonia immune mechanism and especially bacterial inflammatory pathology. It does not imply that every respiratory pathogen produces the same immune profile or that all infections cause purulent exudate. The source provides a mechanistic explanation rather than patient-specific proof.

The page establishes alveolar filling and the occurrence of cough and breathing difficulty in pneumonia, but does not explicitly demonstrate that alveolar inflammatory fluid causes both manifestations. In particular, a causal explanation connecting alveolar exudate to cough is missing. Co-occurrence within a description is insufficient to verify the complete proposed causal arrow.

The passage establishes a specific inflammatory mechanism for dyspnea but does not establish that alveolar inflammatory fluid or pus directly causes cough. Cough appears in a symptom list without a corresponding mechanistic explanation. The detailed mechanism primarily concerns typical bacterial pneumonia and must not be generalized without qualification to every pathogen. The complete two-symptom LINK2 claim is therefore only partially supported.

The passage directly supports the overall infection-to-alveolar-inflammation-and-fluid relationship, but does not identify alveolar macrophages, specific cytokines or neutrophil recruitment. The response is conditional rather than inevitable. Detailed cellular steps require K057S01. The original question-level needs_more_evidence decision is retained independently.
General respiratory infection mechanism; does not independently prove that alveolar fluid or pus causes cough in every pneumonia presentation.
Confirm whether the passage establishes the specific causal transition rather than only describing co-occurring clinical findings.

The source establishes stress and worrying as risk factors but does not quantify stress duration, establish a chronicity threshold or show that every person experiencing prolonged stress develops insomnia. It does not isolate the contribution of stress from other sleep-related risk factors. The specific difficulty-initiating-or-maintaining-sleep phenotype is not separately demonstrated within the Stress section.

The findings are heterogeneous across sleep variables, depression outcomes and populations. Several relationships are bidirectional, outcome definitions sometimes combine anxiety and depression, and important confounders were not consistently controlled. The review does not establish insomnia as an independent causal determinant of later depressive symptoms. Its broader evidence is therefore retained as ASSOCIATED_WITH rather than promoted to the benchmark's RISK_FACTOR_FOR relation.

The included studies were observational and cannot establish causation. Between-study heterogeneity was substantial with I-squared of 92.6 percent, and publication bias was detected. Depression outcomes included both symptom-based measures and clinical diagnoses and should not be treated as identical. The findings relate specifically to insomnia and must not be generalized to every type of sleep disruption. Reverse causation and residual confounding remain possible.

The passage does not explicitly identify DNA damage in lung cells or provide a specific tissue-level mechanism. It also does not specify a minimum exposure duration. Although the narrower tobacco-to-DNA-damage mechanism is directly supported, the complete lung-specific LINK1 relationship is not independently verified.

DNA adduct formation demonstrates chemical injury to DNA but does not establish that every lesion becomes a persistent mutation. Some lesions may be repaired or eliminated. The article supports chronic smoking-related lung tissue DNA injury without specifying an exposure threshold or proving that every exposed individual develops measurable injury or cancer.

The article explains cancer-associated genetic alterations generally rather than specifically evaluating lung-cell DNA damage and subsequent lung cancer risk. Initial DNA lesions are not equivalent to persistent oncogenic mutations. Many DNA changes are harmless, repaired or insufficient to cause malignancy. The exact lung-specific LINK2 relationship is therefore only partially verified.

The source does not establish that an individual DNA adduct or DNA lesion independently predicts or inevitably causes lung cancer. DNA damage may be repaired or eliminated and cancer development generally requires the accumulation and selection of relevant oncogenic alterations. The evidence supports a contributory risk mechanism within tobacco-related carcinogenesis, not an isolated quantitative risk estimate for DNA damage or a deterministic transition to malignancy.

The page directly establishes autoimmune attack, immune-cell accumulation and tissue damage. It does not separately detail the molecular mechanisms of thyroid inflammation or quantify the contribution of individual antibodies and immune cells. Inflammation is supported by the description of immune-cell infiltration and thyroiditis rather than a detailed inflammatory pathway. The extent of tissue damage varies between patients.

The relationship is a possible progression rather than an inevitable consequence of every case of thyroid inflammation. Some patients initially retain normal thyroid function, and the article describes rare transient hyperthyroidism associated with hormone release from damaged tissue. The source does not quantify a specific damage threshold necessary for reduced hormone production.

The passage explicitly establishes thyroid inflammation and reduced hormone production but does not independently describe thyroid tissue damage as a separate intermediate feature. It therefore supports an important part of the composite cause node Inflammation and damage to thyroid tissue without independently verifying both components. The source is retained as partial under strict exact-node adjudication, not because the narrower inflammation-to-hypothyroidism relationship is merely correlational.
